Injection 6 already achieved the maximum CRF, so shorten its gradient while keeping the solvent window and temperature fixed. This tests whether the last peak can elute sooner while preserving R >= 1.5, particularly for the pair previously at R = 1.73.

Shorten the gradient another four minutes with all other parameters fixed to locate the fastest fully resolved method near injection 9. The critical pair at R = 1.59 is approaching the threshold, so this run tests the local resolution limit while retaining a proven maximum-CRF method.
Back off one grid step from the 22-minute gradient to recover full resolution of the critical pair. This should retain the maximum CRF while eluting the last peak slightly sooner than injection 9.

Raise temperature by one grid step while holding the gradient fixed to test whether faster elution can preserve full resolution. Monitor the entire peak pattern for temperature-driven selectivity changes, retaining injection 11 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Test one temperature step beyond the near-coelution at 30 C to see whether the critical pair separates again after an elution-order reversal. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates temperature selectivity and may yield a faster maximum-CRF method.

Shift the solvent window down by 0.05 while preserving gradient slope to test whether increased retention restores resolution of the critical pair at 35 C. This explores solvent-dependent selectivity while retaining injection 11 as the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Return to the successful 25 C temperature and shift the solvent window upward by 0.05, preserving the slope of injection 11. This tests whether stronger starting solvent can shorten elution while maintaining full resolution; injection 11 remains the proven maximum-CRF fallback.

Test a lower starting organic fraction to improve selectivity of the critical pair at 25 C, combined with a steeper gradient to limit late retention. This explores whether a shifted solvent window can retain full resolution with faster elution than injection 11.

Shorten injection 16 by one gradient-time step, using its minimum resolution of 1.98 as margin for faster elution. Keeping the solvent window and temperature fixed will reveal whether full resolution survives the steeper gradient.

Shorten the gradient by another grid step to seek faster elution while retaining maximum CRF. Monitor both the late pair at R = 1.91 and the middle pair at R = 2.27, whose resolution decreased as the gradient steepened.

Test the next shorter gradient to establish the resolution boundary, keeping the solvent window and temperature fixed. The pairs at R = 1.61 and 1.65 are at risk; injection 18 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method if either falls below 1.5.

Shift the four-minute gradient window down by 0.05 while preserving its slope to test whether solvent-dependent selectivity restores the two unresolved pairs. Injection 18 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Trim the unused end of injection 18’s gradient while preserving its slope of 0.05 organic fraction per minute. The gradient reaches the outlet through 4.65 minutes, beyond the observed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this shorter program should preserve full resolution and maximum CRF.

Increase gradient slope modestly from 0.050 to 0.055 organic fraction per minute, between the successful and unsuccessful slopes tested previously. This tests whether the last peak can elute sooner while the critical pairs remain at R >= 1.5.

Reduce injection 20’s gradient slope from 0.075 to 0.0625 organic fraction per minute to improve its two marginal pairs while retaining a four-minute program. This tests another compact maximum-CRF candidate, with injection 21 retained as the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 23’s 0.0625 to 0.0583 organic fraction per minute to bring the late pair above R = 1.5. This targets another fully resolved maximum-CRF method while monitoring the middle pair already close to the threshold at R = 1.59.

Test a two-minute gradient followed by a hold, preserving injection 21’s initial slope through the critical middle peaks while allowing the late peaks to separate during the hold. This explores the shortest programmable gradient; injection 21 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.
